Dorfman (1943), Table I by his formula (not measured): at prevalence p = 1 % the best group size is n = 11 at 20 % of one test per item; at p = 10 %, n = 4 at 59 %; at p = 30 %, n = 3 at 99 %.
note: Relative cost is a share of one test per item; the table ignores test error.

claim: Dorfman (1943) gives two conditions for pooling to pay: the prevalence must be small enough for economies to be possible, and an observation on a group must be easier or more economical than on each individual.

Dorfman (1943): the coefficient of variation of the number of tests becomes small rapidly as the population N increases.

DeWitt et al. (1984), a back-of-envelope figure assuming 10 ms per log write: one log device commits at most 100 transactions per second, and up to ten transactions per commit group give 1000 per second for typical transactions.

claim: DeWitt et al. (1984): a commit group cannot be written, and so cannot commit, until all the commit groups it depends on have committed.

Gawlick and Kinkade (1985), IMS/VS Fast Path: a commit does not wait for the system journal write; the transaction is acknowledged once its journal buffer is written out, when the buffer is full, a time limit expires or standard processing occurs.

Gawlick and Kinkade (1985): by not waiting for the journal write, Fast Path holds critical resources only to the millisecond range, allowing extremely high concurrency; the paper gives no measured figure.

Gawlick and Kinkade (1985): a system journal buffer written out is likely to hold commit records for more than one transaction, so they commit together; the paper says this was named group commit long after Fast Path was built.
